nodes.title: What a model actually is
nodes.blurb: A next-token predictor with no memory, no browser and no soul. Start here.
nodes.mission: Read the first three lessons of Microsoft's beginner course and write down, in your own words, what the model is doing when it answers you.
nodes.why: Almost every frustration people have with AI — it lied, it forgot, it made up a citation — stops being surprising once you know it is predicting the next token from the text in front of it. Do this before anything else.
steps: Open Generative AI for Beginners and do lessons 1-3. Skip the Azure setup for now.
Write a paragraph answering: where does the model's knowledge come from, and what does it not have access to?
List three things you assumed it could do that it cannot.
done_when: You can explain 'next token prediction' to a friend without notes.
You know why it cannot tell you what it said to you yesterday.

nodes.title: Tokens, context and cost
nodes.blurb: Why length is money, and why the model forgets the top of a long chat.

Count the tokens in a document you actually work with.
Look up the context window and the per-million-token price of the model you use most.
Multiply it out for a realistic day of use.

nodes.title: QUEST: hand it something real
nodes.blurb: Take an actual task off your own list and run it through a model end to end.
nodes.mission: Pick one genuinely annoying task you owe someone this week and complete it with a model, keeping every prompt you used.
nodes.why: Tutorials teach you the shape of the tool. One real task teaches you where it breaks — which is the part you need.
steps: Choose a task with a definite finish line: a summary, a plan, a script, a set of test cases, a translated document.
Do it in a single conversation. Do not start over when it goes wrong — correct it and watch what happens.
Save the transcript. Mark the exact turn where the answer got good.
Write down what you had to tell it that you assumed it would know.
done_when: The task is genuinely finished, not half-finished.

nodes.title: Prompt patterns that work
nodes.blurb: Role, context, examples, constraints, format. The five levers, and when to pull each.
nodes.mission: Work through the Prompt Engineering Guide's core techniques and rewrite three of your own weak prompts using them.
nodes.why: Most 'the AI is useless' complaints are a one-line prompt against a hard problem. The techniques here are not tricks — they are the difference between a coin flip and a reliable tool.
steps: Read the Prompt Engineering Guide's basics, then zero-shot, few-shot and chain-of-thought.
Take a prompt of yours that gave a bad answer. Add: who the model is, what the context is, one worked example, and the output format you want.
Run both versions side by side and keep the diff.
Repeat with two more prompts until the improvement is obvious.
done_when: You have three before-and-after prompt pairs where the after is clearly better.
You reach for examples and explicit formats without thinking about it.

nodes.title: QUEST: build your prompt library
nodes.blurb: Stop retyping. Ten prompts you own, versioned, that do your recurring work.
nodes.mission: Write ten reusable prompts for tasks you do repeatedly, and keep them in a file you can actually find.
nodes.why: Professionals do not improvise every time. A prompt library is the compounding asset of this whole stage — it turns a good session into a repeatable one.
steps: List ten things you ask a model for more than once a month.
Browse prompts.chat for structures worth stealing.
Write each as a template with clearly marked slots for the parts that change.
Store them in a git repo, a notes app, or your tool's saved-prompt feature — somewhere you will look.
Use them for a week and edit the ones that disappoint you.
done_when: Ten templates exist somewhere you can reach in five seconds.
At least three have been revised after real use.

nodes.title: Make it return JSON
nodes.blurb: Prose is unparseable. Schemas turn a chat model into a component you can build on.
nodes.mission: Get a model to return the same valid JSON shape ten times in a row, and handle the time it does not.
nodes.why: The moment you want software rather than conversation, you need output your code can trust. This is the hinge between using AI and building with it.
steps: Define a schema for something small — a parsed invoice, a tagged support ticket, a set of flashcards.
Ask for it three ways: plain instruction, instruction plus example, and your provider's structured-output or JSON mode.
Run each ten times and count the failures.
Write the fallback: what your code does when the JSON is malformed.
done_when: Ten consecutive valid responses against your schema.
A parse failure produces a handled error, not a crash.

nodes.title: Context engineering
nodes.blurb: The skill that replaced prompt engineering: choosing what goes in the window at all.
nodes.mission: Take a task that fails on a long document and make it succeed by changing what you put in the context, not how you word it.
nodes.why: Beyond a certain size, wording stops mattering and selection starts. Everything in the RAG stage is this idea industrialised — meet it here first, by hand.
steps: Find a task where a long input gives a vague answer.
Cut the input to only the relevant sections and rerun. Note the difference.
Try the same task with the relevant sections placed at the very end of the prompt.
Write down your rule for what earns a place in the context window.
done_when: You have a case where less context beat more context.
You can say why position inside a long prompt changes the answer.

nodes.title: Run a model on your own machine
nodes.blurb: Free, private, offline, and a genuinely different feeling once it is running.
nodes.mission: Install Ollama, pull a small open-weight model, and hold a conversation with no network connection.
nodes.why: Local models change what you are willing to try: no bill, no rate limit, no data leaving the laptop. They also make model size viscerally real when the small one struggles.
steps: Install Ollama and pull a small instruct model that fits your RAM.
Chat with it in the terminal, then turn your wifi off and chat again.
Install Open WebUI if you want a browser interface over it.
Give the same hard prompt to the local model and to a frontier model, and compare honestly.
done_when: A model answers you with the network off.

nodes.title: Why it makes things up
nodes.blurb: Fabrication is not a bug being fixed. It is the same mechanism that makes it useful.
nodes.mission: Deliberately make a model produce a confident falsehood three different ways, and learn to recognise the shape of it.
nodes.why: You cannot supervise a tool whose failure mode you have never seen. Induce it on purpose now, in a safe context, rather than discovering it in front of a client.
steps: Ask for a citation on a niche topic and check whether the paper exists.
Ask about something that happened after the model's training cutoff.
Ask it to compare two things where one of them is invented.
Note what all three answers had in common in tone and specificity.
done_when: You have three saved examples of confident wrong answers.
You can describe the tell that makes you check.

nodes.title: A checking routine you keep

steps: Draft three checks: are the facts sourced, are the numbers recomputed, would I sign my name to this?
Add a domain-specific fourth check for your own work.
Stick it where you will see it, and apply it for a week.
Adjust it after the first thing it catches.

nodes.title: Automate the right thing
nodes.blurb: Frequency times annoyance minus the cost of it going wrong.
nodes.mission: Audit your week, score every repetitive task, and automate only the ones that clear the bar.
nodes.why: Most abandoned automations were never worth building. Ten minutes of arithmetic beforehand is what separates a tool you keep from a weekend you lost.
steps: List everything you did more than three times last week.
For each: how long it takes, how often, and what happens if it is done wrong.
Cross out anything where a wrong answer is expensive and unnoticeable — those need a human.
Rank what remains and build only the top two.

nodes.title: QUEST: chat with your own documents
nodes.blurb: Upload a folder, ask questions, get answers with sources — without writing code.
nodes.mission: Stand up Dify or Open WebUI, load a document set you actually care about, and get sourced answers out of it.
nodes.why: This is retrieval — the single most useful pattern in applied AI — and you can have it working today. If you later take the engineer path, you will already know what it should feel like.
steps: Install Dify (or Open WebUI with its document features).
Load 20-50 documents you know well enough to grade the answers.
Ask ten questions, including three you know are not answerable from the set.
Check that every answer cites a real source, and note what it does with the unanswerable three.
Tune chunk size or the prompt until the unanswerable ones get refused rather than invented.

nodes.title: Stop it doing damage
nodes.blurb: Approval steps, spend caps, dry runs, and a log you can read on a bad morning.
nodes.mission: Add a human approval step, a rate limit and a log to the automation you built.
nodes.why: An unattended loop with a model in it and write access is how a small mistake becomes two hundred small mistakes. Put the brakes in before you need them.

Cap how many times it can run per hour.
Log every run with its input and output somewhere you can search.

nodes.mission: Route your existing code through LiteLLM and run the same prompt against three different providers.
nodes.why: Prices move, models get deprecated, providers have outages. A one-line model swap is cheap insurance and makes honest comparison possible.
steps: Install LiteLLM and point your existing call through it.
Run one prompt against a frontier model, a cheap model and a local one.
Compare cost, latency and quality on ten real inputs.
Add a fallback so an outage on the primary degrades instead of failing.

nodes.blurb: Screenshots, PDFs, recordings. Often the difference between a toy and a tool.
nodes.mission: Send an image and a PDF into a model and get structured data back out.

Transcribe a voice memo with Whisper, then summarise the transcript.
Measure how the accuracy compares to the text-only pipeline you would otherwise have built.

nodes.title: Embeddings, concretely
nodes.blurb: Text becomes a vector; close vectors mean similar meaning. That is the whole trick.
nodes.mission: Embed a few hundred of your own sentences and find the nearest neighbours of ten of them by hand.
nodes.why: Retrieval feels like magic until you have looked at the numbers. An afternoon with cosine similarity turns RAG from a black box into arithmetic you can debug.
steps: Install sentence-transformers and embed 200-500 sentences from your own data.
Write a nearest-neighbour search with plain cosine similarity — no vector database yet.
Look at the top five matches for ten queries and judge them yourself.
Find a case where the nearest vector is not the right answer, and work out why.
Compare a small local embedding model against a hosted one on the same queries.
done_when: You have written similarity search yourself, without a library doing it for you.
You can name a query where embedding similarity fails.

nodes.title: Chunking, the unglamorous half
nodes.blurb: Most bad RAG is bad chunking. Where you cut the document decides what can be found.
nodes.mission: Chunk the same document four ways and measure which one answers your questions best.
nodes.why: Teams spend weeks tuning prompts when their retrieval was doomed at the splitting step. This is the highest-leverage boring work in the field.
steps: Take one document set and write ten questions you know the answers to.
Chunk it four ways: fixed size, fixed size with overlap, by heading, and by semantic boundary.
For each, check whether the chunk containing the answer is retrieved in the top five.
Keep metadata on every chunk — source, heading, page. You will need it for citations.
Pick a winner based on your numbers, not on taste.
done_when: You have a retrieval hit-rate number for four strategies.
Every chunk carries enough metadata to cite it.

nodes.title: Somewhere to put the vectors
nodes.blurb: A dedicated database, or just Postgres. Fewer moving parts is usually right.
nodes.mission: Load your embeddings into a real store, filter by metadata, and time the queries.
nodes.why: Brute force stops working somewhere around a hundred thousand vectors. Knowing what an index actually buys you keeps you from adopting infrastructure you do not need.
steps: Load your chunks into Chroma to see how little setup it takes.
Do the same with pgvector if you already run Postgres — one fewer service to operate.
Run a query filtered by metadata, not just by similarity.
Time the same query at 1k, 10k and 100k vectors.
Read enough about FAISS to know when an approximate index is the answer.
done_when: Metadata-filtered similarity search works.
You can say at what scale you would need an approximate index.

nodes.title: QUEST: build the whole RAG loop
nodes.blurb: Ingest, chunk, embed, retrieve, answer, cite. Every piece, wired by you.
nodes.mission: Build an end-to-end question-answering system over documents you know well, with citations, that refuses to answer when it should.
nodes.why: This is the reference pattern of applied AI. Once you have built it once, most product requirements you will meet are variations of it.
steps: Ingest a real corpus — your notes, a codebase, a set of policies. At least fifty documents.
Wire the pipeline yourself first, then look at how LangChain or LlamaIndex would have done it.
Return citations with every answer, pointing at the actual chunk.
Add the refusal path: when the top match scores below a threshold, say you do not know.
Test with twenty questions, five of which are not answerable from the corpus.
done_when: Every answer carries a citation you can click through and check.
All five unanswerable questions are refused rather than invented.

nodes.title: Hybrid search and reranking
nodes.blurb: Keywords still win for names and codes. A reranker fixes the order. Both are cheap.
nodes.mission: Add keyword search alongside your vectors, then rerank the merged results, and measure the gain.
nodes.why: Pure vector search misses exact identifiers — part numbers, error codes, surnames. Hybrid plus reranking is usually the largest single quality jump available, for a day of work.
steps: Add BM25 or your database's full-text search over the same chunks.
Merge the two result sets with reciprocal rank fusion.
Add a cross-encoder reranker over the merged top twenty.
Re-run the hit-rate measurement from your chunking work and compare.
Check the latency cost and decide whether it is worth it.
done_when: Hybrid plus reranking beats vector-only on your own numbers.
You know the millisecond cost of the reranker.

nodes.title: Measure the retrieval, not the vibes
nodes.blurb: Faithfulness, relevance, context precision. Numbers that tell you which change helped.
nodes.mission: Score your RAG system with Ragas and use the numbers to reject one change that felt like an improvement.
nodes.why: Without measurement, RAG tuning is superstition. The discipline of rejecting a change that scored worse is the thing that compounds.
steps: Build an evaluation set of thirty questions with known good answers.
Run Ragas and record faithfulness, answer relevance and context precision.
Make one change — a different chunk size, say — and re-score.
Keep or revert based on the numbers.
Wire the score run into a command you can execute in one line.
done_when: You have a baseline score and one measured change.
At least one plausible-sounding change was rejected on the numbers.

nodes.title: Retrieval that decides for itself
nodes.blurb: Let the model choose whether to search, what to search, and when to search again.
nodes.mission: Turn your fixed retrieval step into one the model invokes as a tool, with the option to search twice.
nodes.why: A single retrieval pass cannot answer a question that needs two lookups. Making retrieval a tool is the bridge from RAG to agents.
steps: Expose your retriever as a tool the model can call with its own query.
Allow up to three retrieval rounds before it must answer.
Add a step where it rewrites a failing query and tries again.
Compare against your fixed pipeline on multi-hop questions.
Cap the loop so a confused model cannot search forever.
done_when: A two-hop question is answered correctly.
The loop cannot run away.

nodes.title: What an agent actually is
nodes.blurb: A loop, some tools, and a stopping condition. Deflate the word before you use it.
nodes.mission: Work through the first units of a real agents course and write the loop yourself in under a hundred lines.
nodes.why: The word 'agent' has been marketed into meaninglessness. Writing the loop by hand gives you an accurate mental model and immunity to the hype.
steps: Do the opening units of the AI Agents for Beginners course.
Write your own loop: call model, if tool requested run it, append result, repeat until done.
Add a maximum iteration count and a stop condition.
Give it a task that genuinely needs three steps and watch every turn.
Then read how a framework structures the same loop.
done_when: Your hand-written agent completes a three-step task.
You can explain why a loop with no iteration cap is dangerous.

nodes.title: Designing tools a model can use
nodes.blurb: Bad tool descriptions cause more agent failures than bad models do.
nodes.mission: Write five tools with descriptions good enough that the model picks the right one every time.
nodes.why: Tool descriptions are prompts. Vague names, overlapping responsibilities and silent failures are the top three causes of agents that flail.
steps: Write five tools with narrow, non-overlapping jobs.
Describe each one as if for a new colleague: what it does, when to use it, what it returns, what it costs.
Make every failure return a message the model can act on, never a raw stack trace.
Test with twenty prompts and count the wrong tool choices.
Rewrite the descriptions of anything it picked wrong and measure again.
done_when: Twenty prompts, correct tool chosen every time.
Every error path returns something the model can recover from.

nodes.blurb: One protocol so any model can use any tool. Write a server once, use it everywhere.
nodes.mission: Run an existing MCP server, then write your own that exposes something only you have.
nodes.why: MCP turned tool integration from an N-times-M problem into a plug. Writing one server teaches you more about agent architecture than any framework tour.
steps: Work through the MCP for Beginners curriculum.
Run a reference server from the official servers repo and connect a client to it.
Write your own server exposing something local — your notes, a database, an internal API.
Connect it to a client and use it in a real task.
Think carefully about what you are granting access to before you connect anything sensitive.

nodes.title: Graphs, state and control
nodes.blurb: When the loop needs branches, retries, pauses and a human in the middle.
nodes.mission: Rebuild your agent as an explicit state graph with a checkpoint and a human approval step.
nodes.why: A while-loop is fine until you need to resume after a crash, branch on a condition, or wait a day for approval. That is when explicit state stops being ceremony.

Add a conditional branch that takes a different route on failure.
Add persistence so a killed process resumes rather than restarts.

nodes.title: Memory that is not just a long prompt
nodes.blurb: Short-term scratchpad, long-term store, and knowing what deserves to be remembered.
nodes.mission: Give an agent memory across sessions, and a policy for what it writes down.
nodes.why: Stuffing the whole history into the context is expensive, slow and eventually impossible. Deciding what to persist is a design decision, not a library choice.
steps: Add a working scratchpad the agent keeps within a run.
Add a store that survives between runs — retrieval over past conversations.
Write an explicit policy for what gets written: facts about the user, decisions made, nothing else.
Add summarisation so a long history compresses rather than truncates.

nodes.title: More than one agent
nodes.blurb: Sometimes a team of specialists beats one generalist. Often it just costs five times more.
nodes.mission: Build a small multi-agent system, then prove whether it actually beat a single well-prompted agent.
nodes.why: Multi-agent architectures are fashionable and frequently unnecessary. Running the comparison yourself is how you develop the judgement to know which case you are in.
steps: Build a two or three agent team with CrewAI or AutoGen — for example researcher, writer, critic.
Build the same task as one agent with a good prompt and the same tools.
Compare quality, cost and latency across twenty runs.
Note where coordination overhead ate the benefit.
Write your own rule for when you would reach for multiple agents.

nodes.title: Agents that use a browser
nodes.blurb: Clicking, typing, scraping. Impressive, brittle, and worth understanding the limits of.
nodes.mission: Run a browser agent on a real task and document exactly where it falls over.
nodes.why: Browser automation is the most demoed and least reliable corner of agents. Finding the failure boundary yourself is worth more than any demo video.

Give it a multi-step task: search, filter, extract, summarise.

Add a deterministic fallback for the fragile step.

nodes.title: BOSS: ship an agent people use
nodes.blurb: Tools, memory, MCP, guardrails, a UI, and a week of surviving real users.
nodes.mission: Deploy an agent that does something genuinely useful for someone other than you, and keep it running for a week.

Wire it up: three or four tools, memory, an iteration cap, a spend cap.

Put a human approval step in front of anything irreversible.
Give it to two people and watch the traces daily for a week.
Fix the top three failures you observe — not the ones you imagined.

nodes.title: Why demos lie
nodes.blurb: It worked five times. That is not evidence. Here is what evidence looks like.
nodes.mission: Take something you built that 'works' and find its failure rate on fifty real inputs.
nodes.why: Every team that ships AI has this moment: the thing that felt reliable turns out to be seventy percent reliable. Better to find that number yourself, early.
steps: Collect fifty real inputs — not ones you invented while testing.
Run your system over all of them and read every output.
Mark each pass or fail against a written definition of pass.
Compute the percentage. Sit with it.
Group the failures into three or four kinds — that grouping is your work queue.

nodes.title: Build the test set
nodes.blurb: Fifty cases, expected behaviour written down, runnable in one command.
nodes.mission: Turn your failure analysis into an automated eval suite that runs in a single command.
nodes.why: An eval suite is what lets you change a prompt without fear. It is the AI equivalent of a test suite, and it pays back the first time a 'harmless' change breaks something.
steps: Write fifty cases: input, expected behaviour, and how to check it.
Use exact assertions where you can — contains, matches, valid JSON, correct number.
Set up promptfoo so the whole suite runs from the command line.
Record a baseline pass rate.
Run it against two different models and compare like for like.

nodes.title: Using a model as the grader
nodes.blurb: For things you cannot assert. Powerful, biased, and only trustworthy once calibrated.
nodes.mission: Build an LLM judge for a subjective quality, then check the judge against your own labels.
nodes.why: Most of what matters — tone, helpfulness, faithfulness — cannot be checked with an assertion. A judge scales that, but an uncalibrated judge is worse than no judge.
steps: Define one quality precisely, with a rubric and worked examples of each score.
Write the judge prompt and run it over your eval set.
Label thirty of the same outputs yourself, blind.
Measure agreement between you and the judge.
Fix the rubric until agreement is high enough to rely on — then keep spot-checking.
done_when: You have an agreement number between the judge and your own labels.

nodes.title: See inside a run
nodes.blurb: Every prompt, every tool call, every token, every millisecond, searchable after the fact.
nodes.mission: Instrument your app with tracing and use a trace to diagnose one real failure.
nodes.why: Without traces, debugging an LLM app is guesswork with a reproduction cost of ten seconds a try. With traces, it is reading. This is the highest-value hour in the stage.
steps: Add Langfuse or Phoenix to your application.
Confirm you can see prompts, completions, tool calls, latency and cost per run.
Find a failed run in the trace view and follow it step by step.
Tag runs by version so you can compare before and after a change.
Set up an alert or a saved view for the failure mode you care most about.

nodes.title: Guardrails and prompt injection
nodes.blurb: If your agent reads untrusted text, that text is trying to give it instructions.
nodes.mission: Add input and output validation to your app, then try to break it with a prompt injection.
nodes.why: Any system that puts retrieved documents, emails or web pages into a prompt has an injection surface. This is the security topic of applied AI and it is genuinely unsolved — mitigation is the job.
steps: Read the OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications end to end.
Add output validation: schema checks, refusal detection, PII screening.
Add input handling that keeps untrusted content clearly separated from instructions.
Write five injection attempts against your own app and see which land.
Constrain what the tools can do, so a successful injection still cannot do damage.

Tool permissions are narrow enough that injection is not catastrophic.

nodes.title: Attack your own system
nodes.blurb: Automated probing for jailbreaks, leaks and injection, before someone else does it.
nodes.mission: Run garak against your own application and fix the worst thing it finds.
nodes.why: Manual red-teaming finds what you thought of. A scanner finds the categories you did not. Only ever point it at systems you own.
steps: Install garak and point it at your own model or application.
Run the probes relevant to your use case.
Read the report and rank findings by real-world impact, not by score.
Fix the worst one and re-run to confirm.
Add a red-team pass to your release routine.

nodes.title: Read benchmarks sceptically
nodes.blurb: Public scores are marketing until you know what was measured and what leaked.
nodes.mission: Run a standard benchmark yourself and compare your number to the published one.

nodes.title: Make it cheap
nodes.blurb: Prompt caching, smaller models for easy cases, and not calling the model at all.
nodes.mission: Cut the cost per request of something you built by at least half, without losing quality on your eval set.
nodes.why: Cost is the constraint that kills otherwise good AI products. The techniques are unglamorous and reliably deliver large wins.
steps: Measure the current cost per request from your traces.
Turn on prompt caching for the stable part of your prompt.
Route easy cases to a smaller model and keep the big one for hard ones.
Cache identical requests outright — the cheapest call is the one you skip.
Re-run your eval suite and confirm quality held.

Give every tool the narrowest permissions that still work.
